utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We are here today in this case to have a hearing, as provided for in Rule 54 bis, which is held because the Prosecution has filed an application for an order pursuant to Rule 54 bis. That was filed on the 13th of June, 2008, with quite a number of annexes. The Chamber has received two recent submissions, one by the Republic of Croatia and one by the Prosecution in response to that submission. Before we continue and before I give an opportunity to make further submissions, having set out the main purpose of the hearing of today, I would like to have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger, Steve Margetts, Katrina Gustafson, and case manager Donnica Henry-Frijlink for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. As far as the Defence teams are concerned, the Chamber was informed that the accused Cermak and Gotovina have expressed that they did not want to be present during this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Luka Misetic and Greg Kehoe on behalf of General Gotovina. For the record, General Gotovina has waived his right to be present for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then for the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Andrew Cayley and Tihomir Mak for Mr. Cermak, and indeed, Mr. Cermak has also waived his right to be present this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For Mr. Markac. Then Mr. Kuzmanovic, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For Mr. Markac, Goran Mikulicic and Tom Kuzmanovic, Vlado Randunic, case manager, and David Gault, legal assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I see that Mr. Markac is present...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Markac has expressed his wish to be present this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then for the Republic of Croatia. Mr. Krnic, you are the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia in The Hague. You are here representing the Republic of Croatia and you are assisted by...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRNIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is correct. To my left is Mr. Gordan Markotic. He is the chief of the administration for cooperation with international tribunals of the justice ministry of the Republic of Croatia; and to my right is Mr. Ivan Crncec. He's going to be my technical assistant, and he's the chief of the section in the same department of the justice ministry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krnic. The Chamber wondered how to proceed today, especially in view of the rather extensive submissions that were made by the Republic of Croatia and by the Prosecution. The Chamber doesn't think that it would be of great use to have everything repeated. I immediately add to this that the -- both the submissions, to which I have not commented and I have made no reference yet to the content filed confidentially. Therefore, if the parties want to discuss them, either we should agree on the non-confidential character or we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Were you looking for a submission about the general approach to be taken, or did you -- were you indicating that at any given moment you wanted the parties to raise the possibility of moving into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends. If we come to certain issues for which apparently the Republic of Croatia or the Office of the Prosecution has sought confidentiality, then of course, we should go into private session unless the Prosecution or the Republic of Croatia does not insist on confidentiality anymore. And if we are dealing with matters which are not at the basis of the confidentiality, then of course, we could continue. However, we have to verify -- Mr. Tieger, you know for yourself what is essential -- essentially the reason why you sought confidentiality. So you can express yourself on that matter. If, however, you would like to deal with the submission of the Republic of Croatia, of course you should first verify whether that issue dealt with in the submission is something you could discuss in public. The starting point, then, would be that you could not, but of course, on verification with the Republic of Croatia, that might be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I quite understand, Your Honour, and I agree with what I understand as the general tenor of the Court's direction and, in fact, we filed confidentially at least in large measure because of the confidential filing of Croatia, I do believe that many of the submissions can be made public, but we didn't want to compromise their concerns pre-emptively and filed for confidentially on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the information that is contained in the submissions by the Republic of Croatia and by the Office of the Prosecution is so -- is massive and, therefore, the Chamber, of course, having received these submissions only recently doesn't feel that it could go into any detail and further discuss these matters. So for the time being, the Chamber would like to give an opportunity, first of all, to the Republic of Croatia, who is the responding party in these proceedings, to add whatever you would like to add, perhaps to clarify matters which apparently are contentious, seeing the submissions made by the Prosecution. I would then like to give a similar opportunity to the Office of the Prosecution, unless the Office of the Prosecution would prefer to first outline in general terms the request. I don't know whether you would feel any need to do that, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm happy with the Court's suggestion. I just -- one point of clarification. When the Court referred to the submissions of the Republic of Croatia, I take that to mean, but I wanted to make sure that that was the case, the document that was attached to the Prosecution's submissions that was tendered to the Prosecution this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was referring to a document which carries as a stamp on the cover page "UN ICTY Zagreb liaison officer," received the 15th of July and attached to your submission, Mr. Tieger; and we find also attached a translation, an unofficial translation, into English. It is the document which carries a number -- it is dated 14th of July, 2008. The entry number is 514-09-01-08-75, and it's addressed to the ICTY liaison office, Mr. Thomas Osorio, head of the office. That's the document I'm talking about, and I take it THAT all parties have -- are aware of this document. Then finally, of course, Defence teams. A few things have already been submitted in relation to this request for an order. First, to deny it in limine; also, the issue of whether the admissibility of any material produced as a result of this order would be admissible evidence. That is an issue I'd like not to discuss today. I'd like to discuss the content, rather, the response by the Republic of Croatia. And I specifically invite you, Mr. Krnic, also to address the subsidiary requests made by the Prosecution. I don't know whether I still have to list them for you, but the Prosecution asked, apart from providing within 50 days the documents requested; also, alternatively, to make all the documents obtained available to the Prosecution for inspection; to provide the Chamber with a complete list of all documents in possession of the Croatian authorities; to provide the Chamber with a report detailing the specific investigative steps and the results of these steps; and finally, to continue the investigation. Mr. Krnic, may I give you first an opportunity to add, to emphasize, to clarify the position of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRNIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a place from which it would be uncomfortable to speak when I'm standing. Would it be permissible for me to continue to speak and still be seated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRNIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. First of all, Your Honour, one remark relating to the eventual open or closed sessions that you referred to earlier. We completely agree with your approach, meaning that if in the course of my address we come to such a situation relating to the documents, we will suggest moving into closed session. In respect of your main request, I would like to say the following: Why are we here today? We are here to use concrete arguments to repeal assertions by the Prosecution and the lack of foundation made by the Prosecution request to issue a binding order in relation to requests 723 and 739, also known as requests for the provision of "topnistvo" diaries or artillery diaries as well as actions of the Croatian special police. We are convinced that the request by the Prosecution is unnecessary, and it's not functional in terms of the proceedings and, as such, without foundation. The Republic of Croatia does not have a single reason to -- not to hand over the documents sought by the Prosecution if the authorised bodies of the Republic of Croatia could locate these same documents in our archives. We believe, furthermore, that finding the requested documentation - and as you will hear later, a part of that documentation has been found in the meantime - would go in favour of the arguments that we are stating, and that is that during the war operations that are being discussed on the part of the Croatian army and the police, there were no violations of laws of -- and customs of war. So where is the actual problem then? Before providing a direct answer to that question, please permit me to make a few brief observations which are very important in reaching a decision on whether a binding order should be issued in respect of the Republic of Croatia or not. Since its inception at this Tribunal, the OTP has presented Croatia with 790 various requests to date. The Republic of Croatia has responded satisfactorily in 788 such requests. So what remains are only two partially unresolved requests by the Prosecution, and they are these that we are discussing today, and I underline that this is just partially unresolved. The Republic of Croatia has handed over to the Prosecutor's office since the beginning of our mutual cooperation until today 19.500 different documents containing over 100.000 pages only in the section that concerns the Croatian defence ministry. I would like to add the following: The Office of the President of the Republic of Croatia also furnished the OTP with 666 different transcripts; and what is also generally known is that within the same cooperation, the Republic of Croatia has met all of its obligations relating to the hand-over of accused. Along with that, the Republic of Croatia directly opened its archives, and - I underscore - made direct access possible to members of the OTP, which is also the case in this -- in these proceedings, in this case. The above-referred-to facts can serve as proof of so-called full cooperation of Croatia with the ICTY, and this has been repeatedly asserted and affirmed by the chief Prosecutor Carla del Ponte before various international bodies, and these assertions have also been made by Judge Meron and Judge Pocar in their capacity as Presidents of the ICTY, and they have referred to the successful cooperation of Croatia with this Tribunal. On the other hand, the Prosecutor's office will, as the grounds for its assertion on non-cooperation, probably referred to an official note dating from 1999, in which the Republic of Croatia did not accept for a brief period of time such cooperation in relation to the Storm military action because at that time the Croatian parliament had reached such a decision which the government was absolutely duty-bound to follow. But the Prosecution will probably skip over the fact that after that, in 2000, a parliamentary declaration was adopted on the cooperation of the Republic of Croatia and the ICTY, according to which the cooperation was affirmed and, as I mentioned earlier, was implemented in a constructive way. Therefore, the assertion by the OTP made in this case cannot stand that the Republic of Croatia constantly from 1996 until now has been obstructing cooperation with the ICTY and that non-provision of the requested artillery diaries and other documents in this specific case forms a part of this obstruction, because of which a binding request or order is necessary and, also, informing the Security Council and other bodies about this non-cooperation. In relation to this specific request by the Prosecution, it's true that the Republic of Croatia is encountering certain problems, and problems are of the following objective nature: In reference to the so-called artillery diaries, because these military wartime documents were not adequately maintained because of the conditions prevailing at the time and because of some failings in this aspect in our archives, it has not been possible until now to find all the requested documents. Probably, it doesn't exist or some of it doesn't exist in our official archives, but the Prosecutor's office is insinuating, in a way, that these documents have deliberately been taken away or concealed. We cannot accept such accusations. These accusations are something that we most forcefully reject. In order to dissuade the Prosecutor's office about these assertions and the sense of theirs, we have opened an internal investigation in the course of which scores of people have been interviewed; and the result of that investigation was that a considerable number of documents were found, which have in the meantime, a few days ago, been handed over to the Prosecutor's office. The investigation that was initiated is still continuing. It's an internal investigation and is providing much better results than the case would be had we had initiated regular criminal proceedings via the Prosecutor's office of the Republic of Croatia and because we have fewer obstructions in this way in the circles in which -- on which the investigation is focusing. Our objective at this stage is to establish where the chain of possession of these documents -- or the chain of possession of these documents and the activities of the responsible persons. So criminal proceedings at this phase would include all the familiar processing mechanism, dead-lines, and other means which would enable us to find these documents, which would also be the primary interest of the Prosecution. So the initiation of this investigation, which is obviously yielding good results, and when continued to do that in realistic terms, naturally, is the best proof of the decisiveness of the government to fulfil the requests that have been put. Of course, the Prosecution is interpreting this differently, as a reason more to issue Croatia with a binding order because it only seems to be acting under pressure so that only a binding order would force it to fulfil the relevant request. That is why we believe that this Trial Chamber will know how to assess and evaluate the true facts properly and to take into account all the details of our mutual cooperation in the process. When I'm talking about the artillery diaries, I would like to add something more. The OTP constantly says that these artillery diaries are essential and they're a crucial part of the indictment referring to excessive shelling. I have major doubts in terms of this. If these diaries - which are still not there - are crucial for the Prosecution, what is the basis and the grounds for issuing this particular point in the indictment anyway? How come that the Prosecution first issued this particular count in the indictment and only then proceeded to seek evidence and grounds for such an indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krnic, the indictment against the three accused has been confirmed on the basis of prima facie evidence by the Tribunal. So therefore, I don't think at this moment we should discuss whether the Prosecution has brought this indictment. If the Prosecution considers the documents crucial, that could be for the reason that apart from the evidence available that additional documentary evidence could further support the Prosecution's case; and it is not at this moment, I think, subject to discussion whether or not this expression in the submissions by the Prosecution should lead to conclusions as you suggest would be right conclusions. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRNIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The situation is somewhat similar in relation to documents on the special police. Investigations were carried out, and the documents requested by the OTP had very specific numbers, registration numbers. So that has to do with that part of the request made by the Prosecution; because yet again, the OTP marked this as crucial, essential, extremely important for proving that particular count in the indictment. And then, it so happens that this documentation refers to peripheral matters, procuring food, clothing, et cetera. You will receive more detailed information about this somewhat later, Your Honours. Your Honours, in conclusion of my introductory remarks, I would like to propose that the Trial Chamber reject the request made by the Prosecution and to allow the authorities of Croatia to continue their investigation and to continue looking for the documents in the above-mentioned way; that is to say, to continue the investigation that has started yielding positive results and that will primarily be in the interest of fairness, justice, and the just conclusion of these proceedings and, therefore, in the interest of the OTP as well. May I point out yet again that with regard to this particular legal case, the Republic of Croatia has been cooperative, consistent, and sincere. This Trial Chamber knows that in the same proceedings we took the same attitude with regard to orders made to have documents issued to different Defence teams as well as the OTP. Finally, I would like to ask you to give the floor to my colleague, Mr. Gordan Markotic, who will give you some very specific information in support of the points I have made. He will show to you in a very convincing way that the possible issuing of a binding order on the Republic of Croatia is unnecessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Markotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to state the position of the Republic of Croatia in respect of the request made by the OTP to have a subpoena issued. I am not going to repeat everything that has already been stated in the documents that we provided on the 14th of July. However, it is necessary to explain parts of this response that we provided as well as to refer to some other circumstances that are going to give a more complete picture to the honourable Trial Chamber so that they can establish the actual situation with regard to this request of the OTP. Perhaps I will speak at length, but bear with me because I believe this is necessary in order to understand parts of the request of the OTP. At the very beginning, the OTP states in its request that from November 2006 the Republic of Croatia has not been providing the artillery diaries requested as well as documents of the military police. It is true that in November 2006, or to be more precise, on the 10th of November, 2006, Croatia did receive a request from the OTP, number 719, requesting access to archives of the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. What was done in response was allowing investigators of the OTP who stayed in Croatia in January and in April and several other times in the course of 2007; however, the first request was received on the 15th of May, 2007 - 723 is the number of the document - whereas the submission of documents, of documents of the special police, was requested on the 27th of June, 2007, for the first time, and 739 is the number of that document. I think it is necessary to point that out in order to understand what the time sequence was in respect of certain requests that were made and responses that were provided to them. As for insight into the archives of the Republic of Croatia, what is mentioned is that the Croatian authorities restricted access and insight into archives, unnecessarily limiting examinations of documents and also requesting advance requests to have access to archives and certain documents. We believe that on the whole this is incorrect. Namely, from the very outset these were not unilateral restrictions by the state authorities of the Republic of Croatia; rather, the modalities of gaining insight into Croatian state bodies were agreed upon with the representatives of the OTP. As a rule, they were not opposed to those modalities. Namely, they agreed that the officials in the archives also have working hours; that they cannot be at their disposal 24 hours a day; also, that archives cannot take in a large number of investigators at one point in time; and also, that there has to be a procedure that has to be observed in terms of accessing the archives and making the examination of documents as efficient as possible. I would like to point out today that under the same conditions that were confirmed in terms of examining archives with the representatives of the OTP were applied in respect of Defence teams for accused persons in this case. I think it is also important to say that at one point in time we did try to have archives officials available 24 hours a day so that in this way we would yet again show our good will and cooperativeness in respect of the OTP. However, perhaps at one point the OTP was even in a more favourable position than the Defence teams. However, this system of work simply could not function that way, and the representatives of the investigation teams staying in Croatia agreed with that. The last thing that was agreed upon was that investigators be granted access to the archives in the following way, that they be shown all the registers from a given state body; and then on the basis of these registers, they request documents that are of interest to them. After requesting these documents, the archives officials would bring them binders or maps containing the required documents. Additionally, what was made possible was for the investigators to enter the archives premises to see from which particular place those documents were taken, and perhaps they could look left or right and see whether they needed any other documents too. That is how this functioned, insight into the state archives of the Republic of Croatia. I just want to point out once again that absolutely nothing was hidden from the investigators within the scope of our possibilities. We offered the requested documentation to the investigators, of course, if the documents were in the archives in the first place. As for the artillery diaries, annex C of the request pertains to the request for them, and it is stated specifically there that on the basis of the assessments made by the OTP, the Ministry of Defence and the Republic of Croatia have not submitted at least 328 documents consisting of a total of 943 pages of documentation. What we find confusing in this case is on the basis of what this estimate was made and how can this estimate be that specific. How can they envisage even the number of pages of these documents that have not been seen and no one knows whether these documents actually exist or not? When looking at the existing registers of documents, the existence of the requested documentation has not been established. Furthermore, the Ministry of Defence pointed out in all their contacts with the investigators - and I think that that should be noted now as well - is that the fact that some documents are not in the archives is caused first and foremost by the lack of training and education on the part of some military officers of the Croatian army who were supposed to keep documents and to hand them over, but also it is due to the state of war in which the units operated when often the security and safety of documents was neglected in order to carry out the military operation itself as efficiently as possible. After all, in these proceedings some UN officers already stated that they found at certain localities documents of the Croatian army. So we believe that in this way our assertions are not as impossible as the OTP claims. Another thing that is important to point out is that an analysis was made at the Ministry of Defence, and it shows that the OTP bases its estimates on a very small number of documents, namely, for part of the artillery units that were operating in the area of responsibility of the Split Military District. It is for that reason that they infer that the same kind of documents had to be produced in other units too. However, for certain reasons we believe that these assumptions are off-handed ones, and they have not been supported by any documents; rather, there have been no registers showing that such documents were listed. As for these documents concerning artillery operations, there is also a reference to 14 documents which Croatia has already provided to the OTP. On the basis of 14 provided documents, they mentioned that they are still missing, and we find this a bit perplexing; we don't know how this happened. Of course, we are prepared to send those 14 documents yet again, but I would like to remind the OTP that this happened under 723 and these are operative reports that the Operations Group Sibenik submitted to the Split Military District. As for the special police, the OTP insists on 204 documents with exact numbers. These documents were requested and marked by investigators when they visited the archives of the Ministry of the Interior. When checking these archives, first of all, part of the found documents were sent in accordance with request 19 -- or rather, there were 19 documents out of the 204 that were asked for. And further on in the ministry, through the efforts made by the ministry, we found an additional 66 documents from this list of 204 documents, and that means that the total number of documents submitted was 99; that is to say that 105 are still missing. As for the relevance of this documentation, we can agree with the OTP that these are not relevant documents; however, I repeat that these are documents that were marked by OTP investigators who stayed in Croatia. These are documents that pertained to unimportant matters like thank-you letters, training of divers, refunds of expenses, and so on and so forth, that is to say, documents that are truly unimportant. However, we are therefore even more perplexed by this claim made by the OTP that these are 204 documents that are essential for proving General Markac's culpability. The situation's the same with the 105 documents that have not been submitted. As we went through the registers, we saw what the numbers were, and we realized that out of these 105, 20 refer to personnel characteristics and deployments of members of the special police; 16 to the organization of different courses and advanced training; 14 to the allocation of materiel and technical resources; 6 to other matters; 17 to various payments. So out of 105, 72 or 70 percent are documents of this nature. As for the other part of the request for submitting special documentation, and these are all the documents that pertain to documents received by the office of Markac and Sacic, or rather, the documents that were sent from these offices to third parties, so far we have submitted 41 documents pertaining to General Markac and a total of 325 documents pertaining to Mr. Sacic. An objection was raised to the effect that we submitted irrelevant documents, but these are documents that are of the same nature like the 204 that the OTP requested. At the same time, the OTP is challenging the sending of all orders, maps, and other documents pertaining to artillery and special police in the period from the 3rd of August until the 10th of August, 1995, including the list of targets that every artillery unit received, or the chief of artillery, as well as documents that have to do with the positioning of all artillery units including the firing range. I'm quoting this. These are professional expert documents. As for 17 -- 719 (B) dated the 15th of January, 2007, this has to do with Operation Storm, and in this document, in this analysis, what is mentioned is the number of mortars, cannons, howitzers, and missiles that were used and also the number of projectiles, or rather, the amount of ammunition spent. Also, within 546 as far back as the 7th of January, 2004, that is to say four and a half years ago and even more than that, the following documentation was sent to the OTP: The operations plans of the sectors of the special police that pertain to Operation Storm; reports of the sector of special police written during the first four days of Operation Storm; the reports and orders signed by General Markac; and the same kind of orders signed by General Sacic; and also the war diary of the forward command post of Gracac; the sector of the special police; and also the report on tasks carry out on the 25th of August, 1995, sent by General Markac to General Cervenko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speaker be asked to read slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is general experience here that if you read that your speed of speech goes up and the interpreters ask you to slow down when reading. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Report on executed assignments for the 25th of August, 1995, that I mentioned; intelligence reports on internal control of the special police sector dated the 1st of July, 1995, to the 15th; as well as reports of the intelligence and communications centres or resumes of security events from the 1st of July until the 1st of November from numbers 319 on. We believe that a part of the documentation that the OTP still considers outstanding have actually been furnished with this request from the -- dated 2004. I would also like to mention that Annex (E) of the OTP of Request 739 refers to the fact that this request has not been implemented at all, but actually, the real situation is a little bit different. Annex (E) comprises Supplement 1 and Supplement 2. Supplement 1 is on page 2 and 4 and Supplement 2 from page 7 to 14. In their request for a subpoena, the OTP did not mention that Supplement 2 has completely been provided on the 26th of July, 2007, and with some documents from Supplement 1 and additional documents, which the investigators of the OTP marked when they were inspecting the archives of the MUP. But they did they request them officially in their Request 739, but they did request these documents. In reference to the missing documents which have still not been handed over, investigations have been initiated, and they have been going on for some time now. The investigations began from the bottom up because that is how the authorised body of the Ministries of Defence and the Ministries of Internal Affairs believed they would be the most effective. The investigation in the Ministry of Defence notwithstanding, the OTP said that they tried to speak with 15 highly ranked officials of the ministry who refused to be interviewed. I have to note that this was a request of the Prosecution from the 17th of December, 2007, in which these 15 highly ranking officials were referred to as suspects, even though I have to admit because I was at the office at the time it was not clear to us how you could designate a suspect in December 2007 when the UN Resolution 1503 said that all the investigations had to be completed by 2004. We did act pursuant to the request by the OTP, and we did deliver summons to these 15 officers who, using their right as suspects to refuse to be interviewed, actually did so. Later, according to -- pursuant to an agreement between the OTP and the Defence and shortly before the interviews were to take place, the request of the Prosecution in relation to these persons were modified, and it was agreed that they could be interviewed as witnesses. I also wanted to respond to assertions by the OTP that General Sundov confirmed, who was actually interviewed in the capacity of a witness, confirmed that the documents sought by the Prosecution should be in the central military archives. This assertion by the Prosecution is just partially true. General Sundov actually said that the documents were to have been handled pursuant to the regulations in force and that he was convinced that the bulk of the documents were registered and handed over to the central military archive. But he explicitly said that he could not rule out the possibility that individuals abused their access to the archive, kept documents to themselves, and said that he was speaking only about that part of the documentation that he was responsible for as commander of the Knin Military District. On that occasion, he mentioned the problem of badly trained particular or individual personnel members in the Croatian military, which was actually only in the process of being formed at that time. However, I have to mention that investigators at the defence ministry did interview 44 persons -- actually, 20 persons, while 44 persons were interviewed at the Ministry of the Interior. Therefore, during the investigation into the missing documents, a total of 64 persons were interviewed, and I think that this number speaks for itself, and it proves that investigations were not carried out in such a way as to deliberately prolong them or to avoid interviewing certain persons. As part of the investigations, especially in the defence ministry, and since OTP staff before came out with objections that we were unable to find some maps about war activities during Operation Storm which were published in books of certain high-ranking officers of the Croatian army, interviews were conducted with persons who were directly involved in the preparation of two books which are actually the most important ones and which contain most of the documents. These are books "Sve Moje Bitke," "All My Battles," a book by General Bobetko, and the book by General Gotovina, "Assault, Battles, and Operations," "Napadajni Bojevi i Operacije" of the HV and the HVO. In both cases, persons were interviewed who were directly involved in the work on the book as experts and who confirmed that the maps published in the books were drafted later, especially for the purposes of work on the books; and now these are the maps that we can actually see in the books themselves. If I may summarize, the investigations, they were conducted from the bottom up; and as you can see, a large number of persons were interviewed. Some key persons have already been interviewed or are being interviewed about whom the Prosecution also believes that they are key persons; the investigations are continuing, and interviews are planned with everyone that is relevant for the purposes of the investigation in order to establish the actual state of affairs and to establish the truth. His Excellency Mr. Krnic said that Requests 739, 723 have partially been met. In reference to Request 723, as I already said, documents that were not found were not handed over but that 14 documents were actually handed over but which are still considered outstanding. In reference to Request 739, it needs to be said that the request also included Supplement 1 and Supplement 2 and that Supplement 2 has been implemented in its entirety. As for Supplement 1, it contains eight items, and only Items 1 and 2 have partially not been executed and Item 5. As for Items 3 and 4, which relate to records of documents drafted in the office of General Sacic, unfortunately, the register -- document registers have not been found, and so the request was of a descriptive nature. And pursuant to that request, we furnished 325 different documents, and I already referred to that earlier. As for the part of the request by the OTP that relates to intelligent actions from -- intelligence actions from 1996, relating to obtaining documents on actions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and linking these actions with alleged intentions of the Croatian authorities not to provide documents relating to the Storm action in the same way, I really am unable to find any fact that would link these two activities; and for that reason, I'm not going to comment on this at all. I'm not going to comment on the assertions made in the request. One of the key documents that the OTP refers to is the official note from the 28th of July, 1999, on a meeting held at the Ministry of Justice, which official note was drafted by five officers of the defence ministry. First, I would like to object to the term used in the request, the English term used, "minutes," because these are not actually minutes, but it's an official note, in fact. So the term "official note" or "report" would be much more suitable. In any case, the term "minutes" is inappropriate. The term "minutes" would lead to the conclusion that the controversial assertions in the official note are actually conclusions, which, however, is not the case. I repeat, it's a note signed by five officers, where it is stated that it has been concluded that documents would not be provided that would refer to the state policy of the Republic of Croatia, it would not be furnished to the Prosecution, of course, or rather, the orders by General Norac and General Gotovina. The note also states that the person conducting the meeting, deputy justice minister at the time, would inform the Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal about the meeting itself and the conclusions. At the time, the council was the highest organ in the Republic of Croatia entrusted with cooperation with the ICTY. This is just an impression on the part of the person who compiled the note is tellingly demonstrated by the fact that this was never - and I repeat - never discussed at meetings of the Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. Because had that been the case, first of all, it would have been registered in one of the minutes of the council; and secondly, we are sure that the OTP would not omit to deal with these minutes as stated in paragraph 50 of their request, Footnote 28. Also, at paragraph 52 that refers to this meeting, we think that the then-deputy minister of justice is dealt with in an inadequate way. In 2006 and in 2007, she headed the Office of Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. At that time the former chief Prosecutor, Carla del Ponte, submitted reports to the Security Council of the United Nations in which she pointed out the cooperation of the Republic of Croatia, which was generally on a satisfactory level with the OTP. Therefore, it is unclear how she could have done that if the actual state of this cooperation was the way the OTP refers to it in its request. Your Honours, now we get to the confidential annexes, N, O, and P. So I would kindly ask that we move into closed session for a moment for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Markotic, private session would, I take it, meet your concerns, private session meaning that whatever is said is not to be made public, although still the public can see who is in the courtroom, what happens in the courtroom. If you would have any concerns that someone would start lip-reading when you speak, then we could give further instructions as not to show your face when you're speaking. If you insist on that, usually we -- usually in order to protect the content of the hearing we move into private session. But if you think that that's not enough and that by looking at your face people could, then, identify what you said, then I'll instruct the technical staff not to show your face on the screen. As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no need to have my face protected; and if I lower my head too often, then you will realize I am taking into account what you said just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another matter, Mr. Markotic, is that before we move into private session that we are close to a point where we would have to have a break, anyhow. Could you give us any indication as to how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, five or ten minutes. That is what I would need in order to finish my remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that since we had a late start, we also have a somewhat later break, that you would then now continue; but for our interpreters and transcribers, I would have to be confident that you really can finish in five to ten minutes. Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I believe Mr. Markotic invoked the previous Prosecutor's name in connection with impressions about the level, degree, and nature of cooperation of the Croatian authorities. I think it's informative to appreciate that in 2000, she addressed the Security Council and indicated her hope that all problems would be completely removed but noted in particular that when it comes to matters of where Croatia perceives cooperation to implicate its national interests, the level of cooperation and degree of satisfaction is different; and that has, indeed, surfaced repeatedly and characterizes much of the relationship between our requests for assistance and the responses. Now, that is not to say, of course, that it's the -- it has been the Prosecution's claim in its submissions that a level of stonewalling equivalent to what existed in the period between approximately 1996 and 2000 persisted in its entirety. Indeed, had that been the case the repeated assurances by the Croatian authorities to the Office of the Prosecutor that the documents we sought were being investigated, that sincere efforts were underway to locate those documents would and could only have fallen on deaf ears. But we continued to work with Croatian authorities in the expectation that their efforts would indeed be meaningful --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask that all microphones not in use be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- and sincere. And in that respect, I must note that it was unexpected to hear the assertion that the Prosecution's estimate in Annex C of the approximate number of pages of artillery documentation that would have been created and has not been produced is speculative because no one really knows whether these documents actually exist or not. The Prosecution's request for those documents, as the Croatian authorities well know, was grounded on essentially a three-fold rationale, which was identified in our submissions and clearly identified to the authorities, number one, that those documents were a pre-condition for an artillery assault, particularly one of this scale; number two, the guide-lines prescribed the documentation that is required; and number three, the exemplars that we do possess reflect the compliance with those prescribed guide-lines. For example, the submission by the Republic of Croatia mentioned the 112th Brigade. This is a map of that brigade. This is the kind of document that we say has to be produced, was produced, and should have been presented to us, and yet all too few have been, all too few, which indicate a systemic and systematic problem rather than an inadvertent one. And indeed, when we presented Croatian authorities initially with these circumstances, they acknowledged that the documents should exist, and that is precisely why the investigations were undertaken. Now, we've identified some of the problems with the investigation. I'm afraid that this reflects another basis for the failings of that investigation, and that is apparently an underlying assertion that the documents they purport to look for do not even exist. We've asked the Court in our recent submission to look at the nature of that investigation, and indeed, we did so before; but I think it's important for the Court to examine what's happened recently because as we indicated in our submission, a number of factors clearly indicate the basis for the Prosecution motion and the need for the Court's -- for the order that is requested in the application, and that is the flurry of activity that preceded this hearing and that followed the application as well as the nature of the investigation that was undertaken. As we've indicated, much of the investigative efforts were devoted to simply replicating steps that had already been undertaken and need not have been performed: examining the archives, which we had already been advised had been exhausted; in other words, our repeated and thorough search revealed only the documents that we had obtained. We were told by the appropriate authorities that they were unaware of any other documents in the archives, and yet that is one of the pillars of the ongoing investigation. Similarly, the search for a determination about whether or not documents, artillery documentation, of this type would have to be produced, notwithstanding the fact that Croatian authorities have been previously informed and were informed, indeed, in our motion of the basis for the conclusion that such documentation and at such a level would necessarily have to have been produced. We've also cited some of the other factors that indicate the quality and character of the ongoing investigation. That includes the -- not only those who were interviewed and those who were not interviewed, but the nature of the questions that were asked and the nature of the questions that were not asked of those persons who were interviewed during the course of the investigation. Perhaps most significantly, Your Honour, is what has been completely ignored, not only during the course of the investigation as we've asserted but, indeed, during the course of this hearing, and that is that the most single likely explanation for the systematic absence of the documentation has been utterly overlooked, and the Croatian authorities continue to turn a blind eye to the most likely source of the absence of the documentation in the Croatian archives if that is indeed the case. And that is the lengthy, systematic, government-run cover-up of documentation that threatened the perceived national interests of Croatia during the period between 1996 and 2000, and we've outlined some of those efforts to the court. Those were the efforts that were undertaken under the guise of various operations known as Operation or OA Hague, OA Put, OA Arhiv, and it's important for the Court to understand the almost military -- well, it was, indeed, military precision because these were conducted under the auspices of the Ministry of Defence and the foreign intelligence service, operations which, as indicated in a document sent by the assistant minister of defence for security and information to the then-president of Croatia, involve such things as gathering, processing, and protecting documentation that threatened Croatian indictees or potential indictees or Croatian national interests because those were perceived as -- they said explicitly, as ultimately potentially being linked to the top leadership; operations that engaged in efforts, and I'll quote, "When HVO archives became a serious problem in the course of preparation of General Blaskic's defence with respect to the substance of the subpoena and ICTY's requests involving HVO officials, this service in cooperation with the HIS took action and measures to protect the HVO archives." And there are documents which demonstrate how - again, with military precision - in contrast to the claim that inadvertence or clumsiness or lack of training resulted in the absence of documentation were gathered up and were transferred from central Bosnian archives to Croatia, and thereafter, their existence was denied. And when the ICTY and the OTP made requests for those documents, they were denied. Those efforts included providing direct protection to people who were the subject of indictments, that is, hiding them; it included planting agents in the ICTY and secreting original documents from the OTP for counter-intelligence purposes; and it included planting stories in the media in the hope of embarrassing the ICTY. Those are just some of the factors involved and part of the systematic effort to prevent documentation deemed harmful to Croatian indictees or potential indictees or the Croatian national interests from coming to the attention of the ICTY. And yet, despite the fact that we are aware of this because of documentation that came from Croatian authorities - and they are fully aware of this operation and, indeed, it's been published in the media - you don't hear one word about any effort in the course of these investigations to pursue the most obvious lead of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, what you just said, is that still focusing mainly on the period until 2000 or -- because you started saying 1996 to 2000, and then you gave, well, some strong allegations. Would you say that the focus and the emphasis is on that period or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to make our position clear, Your Honour. It is crystal clear that those efforts were engaged in between 1996 and approximately 2000. What happened thereafter, I cannot assert with the same level of confidence, and I would not do so. What I do know and what the OTP does assert is the following, that either those efforts have continued or if they have not, Croatian authorities are currently turning a blind eye to the fact that they occurred and are wholly unwilling to pursue those people who engaged in those efforts in the past. Now, one of the reasons we went into closed session and one of the reasons the document that was -- the documents that were the subject of the closed session discussion were presented to the Court is because they suggested that some of the efforts that had previously been undertaken might persist. I'm not making that allegation, but what I do say is the longer this investigation goes on -- the longer the investigation did go on without any effort to address that reality, the more it suggested acquiescence, either acquiescence with those previous efforts or essentially sliding into precisely the same effort. And in that regard, Your Honour, I'd like also to address the 1999 minutes which have been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Annex M?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to Annex M to the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe so that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The assertion has been made, and I think -- I'm focusing for the moment on those minutes because in some respects they're particularly telling about the nature and character of the ongoing investigative efforts. The assertion was made that those -- the recording of that set, the conclusions from those minutes, are meaningless because they were never discussed at meetings of the Council for Cooperation; and therefore, I think the suggestion was made to the Court that they're some form of speculation and are untrustworthy for that reason. As it happens, however, two days later, on July 30th, 1999, there was a submission to the Office of the Prosecutor by Dr. Zvonimir Separovic, the then-minister of justice, in which we see the implementation of a large number of the conclusions from the July 28, 1999, meeting; and I'll provide the Court with the July 30th submission. But what the Court will see is that Item 1 of the submission by Mr. Separevic, that is, the provision of documentation concerning proceedings against Momcilo Perisic conform to Item 2 of the official note; Item 2 (a) - and I'll go through them quickly because perhaps the precise -- the particulars of those won't be so significant and the Court will be able to make its own comparison - also conforms to Item 1 of the official note; item 2 (b), information on criminal proceedings before the Osijek county court, conform to Item 3 of the official note; item 2 (c) conforms to Item 4 and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in any event, Your Honour, the -- it was interesting in particular to hear reference to meetings of the Council for Cooperation. We'll submit to the Court some of those meetings, but let me recite some of the discussions which indeed did take place at those meetings. At the 31st session of the Council for Cooperation held on October 28th, 1998, there was reference to the fact that Croatia is actually forced to get into the story of war crimes committed by the Croatian army, and the ICTY requests such evidence, and the only thing to do is to negate the right of the Tribunal to process such crimes; also, reference to the fact that "our aim" is to actually postpone the incrimination. At the 32nd session on October 30th, there was reference to the fact that if the council -- or if Croatia dropped the claim that no armed conflict exists, despite the fact -- despite the skepticism about the validity of that claim registered repeatedly by people at those meetings -- well, to drop that, then they would have to answer ICTY requests for plans, movement of troops, et cetera. And "We have already concluded that we did not want to give them that and that is why we went for the unarmed conflict strategy." And at the 33rd session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do we have to go into -- it's clear that you're quite critical about what happened then, and you say you have some material about that, whereas to some extent the representatives of the Croatian government have said that there has been a certain period of time -- I think let's focus on today -- it's clear that you have a different memory of what happened in the past and that you can more or less offer and say, We have material to support that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then let me focus in conclusion, Your Honour, on something that just happened, and that was the investigation into those 28 July 1999 minutes and the interview of people in attendance. As you will note from the submission, those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that those who were there said this does not reflect what --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And moreover, those conclusions couldn't have been reached because there was nothing but good-will to turn over documents and cooperate with the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that is as good and as bad of an argument as any self-fulfilling prophecy. It can be true; it cannot be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's not true in particular, Your Honour, because one of those persons in attendance was someone who was pivotal in the efforts I described earlier, who was assigned responsibility by the assistant minister for defence in charge of security and information, for protecting -- for gathering and protecting documents and keeping them from the ICTY, and who met in fact with General Blaskic and informed him about the rationale that would be used in saying that -- when gathering up all the documents, protecting them, and then saying to the ICTY, We have no documents. And that in just one moment of the investigation reveals why the Court's intervention is necessary and why the application should be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This was in your submission. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was in your written submissions, your -- reference was made to that, as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would be more than happy to supply the Court with the documentation that -- the more specific documentation I just referred to. And finally, I am available for any questions the Court might have, but I wanted to fill my estimate of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Tieger has raised a point, and I believe I should go directly to the evidence that's in before the Trial Chamber, addressing specifically the point that the Trial Chamber should conclude that the most likely explanation is that there is a cover-up, and if I could ask the registrar to please pull up D152, which is in evidence. It was subsequently made a 92 ter submission by the Prosecution. It is the witness testimony of UNMO officer Alexander Tchernetsky. The specific portion of the transcript wherein the Prosecution made this statement in 92 ter submission can be found at the transcript page 3164 starting at line 1, and if we could turn to page 6 in the English of Mr. Tchernetsky's testimony. Starting at the bottom, Your Honour, Mr. Tchernetsky told this Trial Chamber: "Sometime in September 1995, together with another military observer from our sector, I went on patrol, and we wanted to try to get to Grahovo in order to monitor the situation and the dislocation of the Croatian troops there. Not far from Grahovo, we were stopped at the check-point and were not allowed to proceed further. We turned the car and took another road. Some 2 kilometres south-east from V. Mracaj we found the former commanding post" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, are you drawing our attention to the fact that matters were left behind and found, which already is part of the submission by the Government of Croatia, isn't it? They refer to the evidence in this court, and that supports that records was not -- were not kept, and they even --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to look at it, but I think it was in the most recent --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If it did, Your Honour, I only received a copy of that submission this morning, and I have not had the time to go through it, but I am referring -- I was unaware of it, so I haven't read their submission. We weren't served a copy with it until it was appended to the Prosecution's response this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reference was made at least to -- but it's clear you wanted to draw our attention to the evidence which says that everyone was not always guarding its documents as you would expect them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well -- that's the first point. The second point is I have a vague recollection, although I'm not positive of this, but that there was some inquiry - and I'm not sure if it's part of the trial testimony; it could be part of a supplemental information sheet - that Mr. Tchernetsky was asked, and the Prosecution has tried to locate the documents in the UN archives; and similarly, the Prosecutor's office is having trouble recovering documents from the UN archive. I don't think the Prosecution has made the assertion that because the UN's own archives from this period are - and I will state from our own investigation - in a somewhat chaotic state, that the most likely explanation would be, of course, that there is a cover-up within the UN. Your Honour, I can state as someone who is also working on trying to find relevant documents here that, indeed, it has been our experience that the archives in the Croatian state archive are not in a perfect state. There are missing documents, and we have had to work around that problem. I would also just like to add that -- two points. One is that to the extent that there is an allegation being made that there is a cover-up to protect General Gotovina. Obviously, we reject that assertion. I think we can for the sake of argument say that the level of cooperation in this case between a state and one of its own accused has been probably a model at this Tribunal. And finally, with respect to a procedural matter for future, a problem that arises in this context, and specifically concerning what the Republic of Croatia is doing in the field, whatever the Trial Chamber decides to do there is the problem that some of the people that the Croatian police are now interviewing are witnesses of the Defence. To the extent that the Croatian government has a legitimate interest in conducting an investigation to recover its own state documents, obviously, we have no objection or problem with that. We would be concerned, however, that to the extent that those police investigations go outside the scope of looking for documents and start going into matters concerning their assistance to the Defence - in particular, work product, because some of these people as referenced in the submission were artillery officers - we are preparing documents with them for the purposes of this litigation, and we believe that those documents should in no way be submitted either to the Croatian authorities or to the Office of the Prosecutor to the extent they are documents that have been created since 2006, let's say, for purposes of this litigation, and there should be specific instructions on how far that investigation should go because we would consider that to be work product under Rule 70, us working with our own witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is an interesting issue which needs further thought, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why I wanted to raise it right now, Your Honour. It's a concern that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the record. It's on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a -- quite a complex of detailed information. We might not be able to digest everything immediately; therefore, it might be too much. Nevertheless, focusing on some of the main lines, I would have a few questions. The first question, Mr. Krnic, is the following: In your introductory observations, you said, Well, when we were not during a certain period of time as cooperative as one -- as we are now and as we could be expected to be, you said, But Croatian parliament decided that this would be the course. I wondered, it's a legal issue, whether Croatian parliament could take any decisions that would relieve the Republic of Croatia of its obligations under international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRNIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I said I would now like to clarify. The Croatian Assembly or the Croatian parliament, in its resolution on cooperation with the ICTY in Den Haag, in its decision of the 5th of March, 1999, set out from the assumption or decision, I quote, that: "In view of the legitimacy of the anti-terrorist actions on one's own state territory, and we're talking about the military action Flash and Storm, the Croatian Assembly believes that individual crimes committed in connection with that are a matter exclusively for the Croatian justice system." In such historical moments, and now we're talking about 1999, the Croatian state did not recognise the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia over these two military operations, considering them to be conflicts of an internal nature. In its declaration on cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague of the 14th of April, 2000, the Croatian parliament stated, I quote, that: "The Republic of Croatia does not bring into question the right of the Tribunal to establish responsibility for crimes committed during and immediately after the end of the homeland war and will insist that the International Criminal Tribunal in its proceedings processes all of those responsible for war crimes on the territory of the former Yugoslavia." So this was a legal and political question, and I'm speaking about 1999 again. The impunity of those who committed the crimes was not something that was being considered, but the belief was that these crimes would be exclusively in the jurisdiction of the domestic courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, and to some extent you have answered my question in -- to some extent in the affirmative, that where the limits of the jurisdiction of this Tribunal are you say is for the Croatian parliament to decide and not for the Tribunal. That's more or less the implicit message in such a -- in such a decision. But let's not -- I just wanted to -- since you briefly referred to the Croatian parliament reaching a decision, you said, which the government was absolutely duty-bound to follow. Now, I have one other question. Perhaps, Mr. Markotic, you are the one who could answer that. You have given us a number of 64 interviews, a lot of names we find in your submissions of the persons being -- that have been interviewed or are still to be interviewed or whose interviews are still to be continued. Could you tell us what was -- have you recorded the dates of those interviews? Because apparently, one of the issues raised by the Office of the Prosecution is that you became active only at a certain stage. Could you tell us, when was the first of these 64 interviews you're referring to, when was that conducted and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the situation with the interviews. The Ministry of Internal Affairs interviewed 44 people, and 20 were interviewed in the defence ministry. In the defence ministry, 40 informative talks were conducted until February 2008, a few months before the Prosecution requested that a binding order be issued. The other interviews were conducted after June 2008 when another 18 persons were interviewed at the defence ministry and 4 people at the Ministry of the Interior. We said before that information talks were conducted at the Ministry of Defence, but we didn't mention the names of those who were interviewed. In our document of the 14th of July, which you will have an opportunity to see, all the names are reported and the times of the interviews. We also have reports or notes recording all of those interviews and up to February -- of all conversations, interviews committed up to February 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you provided the Office of the Prosecutor with the reports or the summaries or the transcripts, whatever is there, of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We informed the Prosecution that the interviews had been conducted and, in brief, the results of these interviews, but we did not furnish them with the actual transcripts of those interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you have any problem in doing so? Because it seems that there is a rather tense situation between a lack of trust in your honesty, to say the least, by Mr. Tieger, whereas you say, We stress that we do sincerely our utmost best to reach the best possible results. Would this be a matter which you could share with Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, some of those transcripts would first need to be looked over and then provided, but the OTP didn't ask for the transcript but for the status of ongoing investigations, to which we responded. Of course, I am sorry that there is a certain degree of distrust on the part of the OTP, but again, as we heard from Mr. Tieger this is based on the period before 2000. Now we're in 2008, and we can provide this. Of course, we need to receive the appropriate request from the Prosecution, and then we would be able to provide this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear Mr. Tieger say that it was based exclusively on the period until 2000. He has explained that sufficiently, I would say, but I appreciate that you refer to a period on which he extensively sought to inform the Chamber. There is another matter. We have looked in private session to the -- to two documents that were provided to us by the Office of the Prosecution. You've commented on those. We after that, and we were not familiar with that, we heard about a written explanation of what that material was aiming at or at least the -- what was described in this -- in these documents, what these activities were aiming at. Here in this courtroom, the status of these documents have been subject to some discussion. They have been put to us; they have been commented upon. Would you have any problem in the Chamber considering the issue, best efforts against not-good-enough efforts, because that seems to be part of discussion, that we look at that material? Would you have any problem with that? But then, of course, we would like to look at the material to the comments you've given in private session, also to look at the written explanation, and of course, we've heard the interpretation of this material by Mr. Tieger. Would that meet any objection by the Government of Croatia if we would look at all this material?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in closed session we discussed two documents that are referred to in Annexes N and P of the Prosecution's request, and I exclusively referred to them when I spoke. Since we're talking about copies of the documents that are now accessible to the Court, I assume that there will be no problem to show the originals, if necessary, of those copies that have been provided. Of course, they're identical. I will still need to consult with the agency that drafted the documents, but we can furnish all the documents that I referred to when I cited the documents, and that is actually the response or the responses of Croatia to the requests from the OTP that I mentioned to carry out similar activities as requested in the incriminating document from Annex P of the request for the issuance of the binding order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, the Chamber would not oppose if you would send us documents, requests you received earlier from the Prosecution you referred to. However, the focus of my question was, these two documents we discussed, these are the annexes - let me just check them again - it's O and P, Annexes O and P to the initial request, whether we look at that in order to -- as part of our preparation in reaching a decision; that's one. And then we would then invite Mr. Tieger, also, to provide us with what apparently is a written explanation about the oral explanation. Mr. Tieger, I'm a bit hesitant because if it's not recorded, audio-recorded, I mean, then, of course, you would get perhaps information which might not be shared by all those who took part in such conversations, but at least to have a look at the written explanation the Croatian government has given to the OTP about these two annexes, O and P.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems to me that along with Annexes O and P we're talking about this official note, as well, that Mr. Tieger referred to today, and in relation to that he mentioned the statements made by some Croatian officials in 1999. As regards these annexes, O and P, there are two documents of the Croatian intelligence agencies that we will try to submit, of course in a manner that we will agree upon with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My problem -- you're referring to these documents. We are not -- at this moment, we are mainly interested in considering the content rather than to receive original documents. If you say what was attached as O and P, the content is the same as we find in the original, then we're not insisting on having the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the content of these original documents is the same like what is contained in the confidential annexes. I oriented myself -- similar requests of the OTP, and the agency acted in the same way. The documents are the same, originals, and from the annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we don't have an authenticity problem in relation to the Annexes O and P to the Prosecution's motion. That's clear. Then we would then ask Mr. Tieger to provide us with the explanation given by the -- you refer to the written explanation given by the Croatian government. Then another matter raised. Mr. Tieger, Mr. Markotic says -- you asked for documents being very important, and then although we have not provided all of them, now we have provided at least some of them, and you say they are of hardly any importance. That's part of -- I summarize of course. Do you have a response to that, where you, I think, qualified all the documents as either relevant, highly important, that those produced now are dealt with as not of great importance?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's dealt with in the submission, Your Honour, in this sense and in two ways. The relevance of a document is -- before it's seen is identifiable by its date, source, intended recipient, general nature. The issue here, as far as the OTP is concerned, is our request for a large number of documents and our receipt of a relatively small number of those -- small percentage of those documents, and those documents that we do receive appear to be of relatively peripheral significance. Now, that's significant on its face, I submit, and it's also particularly significant in light of the pattern of conduct we can see from the documents relating to the treatment of these materials in the past, and that is there were explicit directives to provide the OTP or the ICTY with material that was of a relatively harmless nature and didn't implicate the national interests of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, that's -- I'm not saying that the past is irrelevant, but that's at least in its full explicit form. That's -- we are looking back a few years from now. Because you also -- you used one argument, saying that -- well, if you think that or if you claim the documents do not exist, it comes as no surprise that if you start looking for them that you don't find them. You use that as an argument as in the context of bad faith. Now, I asked myself --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Or, Your Honour, bad faith or the -- I guess, commitment to the effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- well, no commitment to the effort, of course, is a form of bad faith, perhaps, as well. Now, I asked myself if someone believes that a document doesn't exist and he doesn't start looking for it, then he'll be blamed not looking for it. Now, if he says, I don't think it exists but nevertheless, I'll start looking for it; the argument then is, Well, no wonder that you don't find it because you believe they don't exist. So therefore, you must have been looking not seriously for them. I'm just asking myself how fair that reasoning is. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would point the Court in a somewhat different direction, and that is when there is a solid basis for asserting that the documents exist, and I tried to articulate that on the basis of the guide-lines and so on, and your interlocutor initially agrees that that reasoning is sound and the exemplars you receive demonstrate that that reasoning is sound, then a reversal of that position strikes me as significant. And Your Honour, if I could raise one minor point. I want to dispel any misimpression that the Prosecution wasn't interested in the investigations. We undertook a mission in May, in fact, to find out what was happening with the investigations and as much as we could learn about what had been done and were explicitly told that we couldn't get that information because it was precluded by law. So if that's not the case, that's a good thing; but the fact that we don't have -- we didn't have information about the investigations prior to the recent submission was not the product of any lack of interest or lack of effort but despite that interest and effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's anything you'd like to briefly add to what has been said, you have an opportunity to do so, but let's try to limit it, Mr. Krnic, to not more than three to four minutes. But if you say everything has been said what should be said, then we'll conclude this hearing. Your microphone is still open, and although it's not translated to us, everyone could hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRNIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we absolutely stand by all the assertions we made here. We underline, once again, that we spoke openly, sincerely, and without any ulterior motives. We are also aware of the following, and that is the problem, and that is shown by what the Prosecutor said today unequivocally. The Prosecutor does not want to admit that the additional efforts that we have made have contributed to the finding of certain documents and that we have the best of intentions of continuing down that road. And then, to ask for a binding order, this objectively brings into the question the efforts that are already being made. Why? Because the Prosecutor is insisting on criminal charges against certain persons. Criminal prosecution has a lawful course of its own; it is only going to slow down the efforts that we're making right now. If I were to say anything else in terms of Croatia giving countless examples of good-will, in terms of cooperating with the Tribunal, that is, that would just be repetition. Therefore, I would like to end my remarks on that note. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krnic. This concludes this hearing. Mr. Krnic, Mr. Markotic, and Mr. Crncec, I'd like to thank you very much to have come to this hearing and present the position of the Republic of Croatia. This Chamber would find it more difficult to make determinations if it would not have heard the views of the state concerned. Therefore, thank you very much for coming. We adjourn and we will resume Monday, not for you but for the case itself. We'll resume on Monday, the 21st of July, at 9.00 in the morning in courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of July, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [The Accused Gotovina and Cermak not present]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.31 p.m.,
